name: The Learning Trap
title: The Learning Trap
answer: The Learning Trap is the risk that AI lets students complete work without doing the thinking that builds lasting knowledge, and it often goes unnoticed by everyone, including the student. It matters because the assignment gets finished while the learning does not, and students cannot tell the difference on their own.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea describes a quiet failure mode of AI in education. When a student struggles with a math problem, redrafts a paragraph, or tries to put an idea into her own words, that effort is what makes knowledge stick. An AI tool can erase that struggle in seconds, so the product looks fine while the learning never happens. The trap is hard to catch because grades and finished work can improve even as understanding drops. The problem it solves is misdirected attention: schools worry most about cheating, when the deeper risk is skipped thinking.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Schools can design around much of the trap by building assignments so students have to think, using the five moves shown in Figure 1.5, none of which needs special software. The text does not break those moves down by grade band beyond one clear rule for the early years. In the early grades, most AI use should sit with the teacher, who applies it to planning and preparation rather than handing it to the child. In later grades the same principle holds through assignment design, where the task itself requires the student's own reasoning. The common thread is that the thinking stays with the student and the tool does not replace it.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with evidence from two studies. The Turkish math study showed practice scores rising while real learning fell, and students could not tell the difference. A second study came from a German platform that gave AI feedback on writing to more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12. Nearly half of them, 48 percent, did not change a single character of their work after reading the feedback, and the rate barely moved from first grade to twelfth (Jansen et al., 2025). The book's point from this is that feedback nobody acts on teaches nothing, however good it is.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about what design can and cannot fix. The text says schools can design around much of the trap, which means some of it remains, and the risk is that skipped thinking goes unnoticed by teachers and students alike. The decisions that stay with people are the assignment design choices, since the five moves require no special software but do require that the work be built so the student has to think. For younger children the text sets a firm boundary: in the early grades most AI use belongs with the teacher for planning and preparation, not with the child. Nothing in the text removes the teacher's judgment about when a task should carry productive struggle.
